phonemes.desc: Unaspirated voiceless bilabial stop [p] plus long upsilon with acute/circumflex [ŷː], followed by rho. The whole word is one long, high-pitched syllable.

pronunciation.approximation: 'PYOOR' — one long, high-pitched syllable, like the sound of a flame catching.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *péh₂ur, 'fire'; cognate with English 'fire' and Hittite pahhur

pronunciation.note: Pŷr is Tier 1 because the Greek πῦρ contains both length (υ) and stress (acute/circumflex) on the same syllable. It is one of the oldest and most culturally charged words in Greek.

domains.title: Fire
domains.subtitle: Transformation, Purification, Cosmic Process
domains.lead: Pŷr is the Greek word for fire, an element that transforms, purifies, destroys, and illuminates. For Heraclitus it is the very substance of becoming; for cult it is the medium through which mortals communicate with gods; for tragedy it is the price and the door of immortality.

cards.name: Heraclitean Flux
cards.desc: Heraclitus made fire the arche: all things are an exchange for fire, and fire for all things.

cards.name: Sacrificial Flame
cards.desc: Greek worship centered on altars where fire carried offerings upward to the gods.

cards.name: Purification
cards.desc: Fire cleanses metals, bodies, and cities; it is both punishment and renewal.

cards.name: Light in Darkness
cards.desc: The torch, the hearth, the beacon: fire as knowledge, safety, and communication.

symbols.name: Flame

symbols.name: The fennel stalk

mythology.lead: Pŷr is elemental and mythic at once. It is the stolen gift of Prometheus, the cosmic arche of Heraclitus, the threshold-light of the mysteries, and the fire on Mount Oita that burned a mortal into a god.

myths.title: Prometheus Steals Fire
myths.text: At Mecone, Prometheus tricked Zeus in the division of the sacrifice, wrapping the good meat in the ox's paunch and the bones in a layer of glistening fat; Zeus, seeing through the trick, chose the fat — and in anger withheld fire from mortals (Hesiod, Theogony 535–570). Prometheus stole it back, hiding the flame in a hollow fennel stalk and carrying it down to earth. Zeus answered with a two-fold punishment: he bound the thief to a crag in the Caucasus, where an eagle daily devoured his regenerating liver, and he had Hephaistos mold the first woman, Pandora — a 'beautiful evil' — whose jar released every affliction upon the human race (Works and Days 50–105). Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound dwells on the theft's aftermath and the catalogue of gifts — not fire alone but hope, medicine, number, and the arts. Fire is civilization's founding theft, and the myth prices it at an eagle's daily meal: every human warmth carries a debt somebody else is paying.

myths.title: Fire as Cosmic Arche
myths.text: Heraclitus of Ephesus declared that 'this ordered world, the same for all, no god made nor man, but it ever was and is and shall be ever-living fire, kindling in measures and going out in measures' (DK 22 B30). All things are an exchange for fire, and fire for all things, 'as goods for gold and gold for goods' (B90); even the sea is liquefied and measured fire. Strife, want, and surfeit are the measures by which the flame stays alive; the thunderbolt — purest fire — 'steers all things' (B64). Aristotle reports the doctrine at Metaphysics 983b and made fire one of his own four elements, while the Stoics converted Heraclitus' ever-living fire into the logos-pneuma that permeates and governs the cosmos, a conception Cleanthes hymns in his Hymn to Zeus. To call the world fire is to call it a verb: the only element that is pure process, whose identity is transformation itself.

myths.title: Fire in Initiation
myths.text: When Demeter searched the world for her stolen daughter, the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (47–50) gives her burning torches, wrenched from the volcanoes of Aetna — fire as the grief that searches the dark. The mystery rites at Eleusis built on that image: torchlit processions along the Sacred Way from Athens, lamps and blazing bowls in the night rites, and the fire that marked the boundary between the uninitiated and those who had seen. Plutarch compares the experience of the mysteries to the soul's passage at death, and Lucian's account of Alexander of Abonoteichus shows how cheap the imagery became when copied without awe. Fire at the threshold does not illuminate fully — that would profane — it marks the crossing: the initiate walks from torchlight into darkness and back, and the flame is the proof that someone carried light through on their behalf. The mystery made fire the syntax of secrecy: visible from far off, unreadable up close.

myths.title: The Pyre on Oita
myths.text: Heracles, poisoned by the blood of the Hydra on the robe his wife Deianira sent him, commands his son to build his funeral pyre on the summit of Mount Oita (Sophocles, Trachiniae 1191–1278; Apollodorus, Library 2.7.7; Diodorus Siculus 4.38). The poison is burning him alive from within, and he longs for the fire to finish what the robe began — but no mortal dares light it. In the common version the archer Philoctetes (in some accounts his father Poeas) kindles the pyre and receives the great bow in payment; as the flames rise, a cloud takes the hero up, and from the pyre's heart he is received among the gods on Olympus. Ovid tells it with terrible beauty at Metamorphoses 9.229–272: 'I, who conquered a thousand monsters, am conquered by the poison I myself once conquered.' Fire is the only element that can do what the gods alone require — consume the mortal part and release the rest. The pyre turns death inside out: what it destroys is the body, what it saves is the man.

lore.syncretism: Pŷr became one of the four Aristotelian elements and the Stoic active principle (pneuma/fire). Zoroastrianism elevated fire as the purest symbol of Ahura Mazda, tended in temples where it must never be polluted. In Christian symbolism fire became the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, judgment at the end of time, and the refining flame of purgatory. The Greek word survives in English through 'fire' itself, 'pyre,' and the scientific family of 'pyro-' compounds — pyrotechnics, pyroclastic, pyromania — while modern chemistry defines fire as rapid oxidation and smiles at the metaphysicians. But the cultural symbolism remains ancient: every rocket, furnace, and candle still speaks Heraclitus' language, promising transformation at a measured cost.
lore.culturalLegacy: Pŷr is the element that made us human: cooking, metalworking, ceramics, glass, steam, electricity, and rocketry are all chapters in the domestication of the flame. Prometheus' theft is the founding myth of every technology — power taken from nature and turned against scarcity. Yet fire is also the element we most fear: conflagration, war, cremation, and the climate's slow burn. The Greeks kept both truths in one word. Hestia's hearth anchored the home and the state; the prytaneion's perpetual flame was the city's heartbeat; the Olympic flame still runs relay across the world as a moving fragment of that ancient fire. To hold pŷr is to hold the origin and the end of civilization in the same hand.
lore.extendedMeditation: Pŷr is the most alive of the elements. Earth rests, water flows, air moves, but fire consumes and transforms; it is never the same from moment to moment, and that is its definition. Heraclitus saw in it the logos of the universe — not a substance but a rate, a measure, a way of burning. Fire also teaches danger and responsibility together. Prometheus was punished not for discovering fire but for giving it away without a warranty, and every technology since has repeated his dilemma: the gift warms the household that it might also burn. To honor pŷr is to respect both its generosity and its hunger — to use it without being consumed by it, and to remember that it is always exchanging us, in measures, for itself.

lore.archaeology: Fire was the organizing technology of Greek cult: every altar maintained a flame, and the ash-and-bone altars (escharai) of heroes and the great burned-offering deposits of the gods are among the most common finds at sanctuaries. The heroön at Lefkandi (Euboea, ca. 950 BCE) preserved a warrior's cremation on a pyre inside its great hall — archaeology's earliest witness to the pyre as a door. Hephaistos' forge and Prometheus' theft were painted on hundreds of Attic vases; the eternal flame at Olympia and the prytaneion hearths of cities like Athens were maintained by civic officials as the state's perpetual fire. Kilns, smelting furnaces, and domestic hearths mark nearly every excavated Greek site — fire was the first infrastructure.
